content: Painful bladder syndrome, also known as interstitial cystitis, is a chronic condition that predominantly affects women, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 10:1. It is characterized by symptoms such as pelvic pain, urinary urgency, increased frequency of urination, and nocturia (waking up at night to urinate). The diagnosis of interstitial cystitis is often based on cystoscopic and histological findings, but in many cases, it is a diagnosis of exclusion, made after ruling out other potential causes like infections or malignancies. This has led to the broader term painful bladder syndrome being used in cases where specific diagnostic criteria are not met. Overactive bladder (OAB) can present with similar symptoms, such as urgency and frequency, but it lacks the defining symptom of pain, which is central to painful bladder syndrome. The prevalence of painful bladder syndrome varies widely across populations, ranging from 8 cases per 100,000 individuals in the Netherlands to 500 cases per 100,000 in certain regions of the United States. This variability is partly due to differences in diagnostic criteria and the investigative methods used to confirm the condition. The strictest diagnostic criteria for interstitial cystitis are those established by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK). These criteria require both cystoscopy and cystometry to exclude other potential causes of symptoms. They also specify minimum requirements for patient age, symptom duration, urinary frequency, and nocturia. While these criteria have been useful for research purposes in identifying a relatively homogeneous group of patients, their applicability in routine clinical practice remains controversial. A specific finding during cystoscopy, known as Hunner's ulceration, is included in the NIDDK criteria and is used to distinguish between ulcerative and non-ulcerative forms of the condition. These subtypes differ in terms of their underlying pathophysiology and prognosis. The exact pathophysiology of painful bladder syndrome is not fully understood, but it is increasingly recognized as a multifactorial condition. A loss of integrity in the bladder's epithelial lining, potentially triggered by an infection or inflammatory insult, is thought to play a key role. This may be accompanied by upregulation of sensory nerves and increased activation of mast cells. The resulting process can lead to a form of regional neuropathy, which may manifest not only as bladder-related symptoms but also as gynecological and gastrointestinal issues. In some cases, the presence of antinuclear antibodies and the clinical course of the disease have suggested an autoimmune component to its pathogenesis. The multifaceted nature of the condition has led to the development of a wide range of treatment options. These include oral medications, intravesical (bladder instillation) therapies, dietary modifications, lifestyle changes, nerve stimulation techniques (peripheral or transcutaneous), and surgical interventions. Often, combinations of these treatments are employed to maximize therapeutic benefits. This discussion focuses on oral medications used to manage painful bladder syndrome, with a systematic review of intravesical treatments currently underway. The following oral treatments are commonly used for interstitial cystitis, along with their proposed mechanisms of action: 1. Pentosan polysulfate: This medication reduces the permeability of the bladder mucosa to potentially toxic components in urine and inhibits histamine release from connective tissue and mucosal mast cells. 2. Hydroxyzine: This drug prevents mast cell degranulation and has additional muscle relaxant, antihistamine, anticholinergic, and analgesic properties. 3. Benzydamine: A non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agent. 4. Steroids: These medications exert anti-inflammatory effects. 5. Cimetidine: A histamine H2-receptor antagonist. 6. Oxybutynin: An anticholinergic agent that helps reduce bladder spasms. 7. Amitriptyline and other tricyclic antidepressants: These drugs have anticholinergic, analgesic, and potentially antihistamine effects. 8. Rifampin: An antibiotic. 9. Antibiotic regimens: These may include sequences of antibiotics such as doxycycline, erythromycin, metronidazole, clindamycin, amoxicillin, and ciprofloxacin. 10. L-arginine: This compound acts via the nitric oxide pathway to relax smooth muscle and reduce pain. It may also have immunological effects. 11. Recombinant human nerve growth factor: A potential therapeutic agent under investigation. 12. Flavoxate: An antispasmodic agent. If additional oral medications not listed here are identified during ongoing reviews, they will also be evaluated, provided they meet the inclusion criteria for clinical trials.
